new_statements.quote: Stress. In Speedwords of more than one syllable the stress always occurs on the first syllable, except in the cases of opposites ending in -o (second half of this lesson) and words having the prefixes y (lesson 6) and u (lesson 10). [DWS p. 14] || 379. In Speedwords of more than one syllable the accent is placed on the first syllable. For instance, the accent in axl (shown by heavy type), is ax(i)ll just as in the English word "axle" it is ax(u)ll. Similarly ofi is offee like the accent in the English word coffee. 380. In the following cases, for special reasons, the accent is not on the first syllable. (1) When a Speedword opposite ends in '-o' ... The syllable containing the '-o' is therefore always accented: e.g. supo = suppoh ... (2) When the 'y-' or 'u-' prefixes are added ... the normal accent is retained: e.g. ofi = offee, uofi = ungoffee, yofi = y-offee [Companion p. 24]

Both read from the page photocopies reproduced in Raymond Brown (2019), 'Dutton Speedwords Pronunciation', pp. 1 and 3.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root in every polysyllabic word. Two systematic exceptions: (1) the 'opposite' suffix -o always carries the stress (supo = sup-PO, imof = im-MOF), even when further suffixes follow; (2) the verbal prefixes y- (past/perfect) and u- (present participle) are extrametrical — they never take stress, the root keeps its initial stress (yofi = y-OF-i). Wikipedia (citing DWS p. 62 §308) adds that the comparative/superlative prefixes me-/my- are likewise unstressed. In idea-compounds the accent is on the first component (§377).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Opposites in -o take the stress on the -o syllable; prefixes y- and u- (and, per Wikipedia citing DWS §308, me-/my-) are never stressed; compounds accent the first component (with linking -ing/-ng/-ish syllables inserted).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for a designed auxiliary language; stated for 'Speedwords of more than one syllable', including derived and compounded words. Description is prescriptive (invented language), 1946 edition; the 1951 revision changed some roots but no later source revises the stress rule. Single-letter particles carry unwritten vowels and are not covered by the rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog dutt1234 = Dutton (World) Speedwords, an English-based constructed auxiliary language / briefscript by R. J. G. Dutton (1943–1951 editions; 'Teach Yourself' 1951/1971). The stress rule is Dutton's own prescriptive rule for the 1946 (3rd-edition) form of the language; the 1951 revision changed roots but no examined source changes the stress rule. Not a natural language; stress statement is prescriptive design, not observed speech.

sources.note: 'STRESS. Generally on the first syllable of a word. Exceptions: (a) the suffix -o, _always_ takes the main stress. (b) the verbal prefixes u- and y- are never stressed.' Compounds: '(Stress stays on first syllable).' (paraphrase of Dutton; Brown's later PDF says this page contained typos and goes back to the photocopies)

sources.note: §379: accent on the first syllable in words of more than one syllable (axl = AX(i)ll, ofi = OFFee); §380: not on the first syllable (1) in opposites ending in -o, whose -o syllable is always accented (supo = suppOH, imof = immOFF), (2) y-/u- verbal prefixes do not shift the normal accent (uofi = ungOFFee, yofi = y-OFFee); §377: in idea compounds the accent is on the first component
